claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are predominantly governed by grain-boundary strengthening from grain refinement.
Grain refinement increases hardness and strength through the Hall–Petch effect.
Lattice distortion inherent to multielement high-entropy alloys inhibits dislocation motion.
Grain-boundary strengthening and lattice-distortion strengthening act synergistically to enhance hardness and yield strength.
Processing that reduces grain size without extensive secondary-phase precipitation markedly improves mechanical properties.
A coarse-grained, single-phase BCC high-entropy alloy can serve as the baseline state.
The proposed baseline has moderate lattice strain.
Irradiation can alter and, under some irradiation conditions, refine the grain structure of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Keeping bulk composition and chemistry constant avoids the formation of extensive secondary precipitates during processing.
Reducing average grain size increases grain-boundary area.
The refined-grain alloy should have significantly greater hardness than the coarse-grained baseline.
The hardness increase from grain refinement could be several GPa.
The refined-grain alloy should have greater yield strength than the coarse-grained baseline.
Hall–Petch strengthening should persist only down to a critical grain size, below which softening mechanisms may operate.
The coarse-grained baseline has a moderate hardness of approximately 13–15 GPa.
Secondary-phase formation can materially influence hardness in a high-entropy alloy.
Elevated temperature may introduce additional influences on strength beyond the proposed room-temperature grain-refinement mechanism.
The relative contributions of grain boundaries and lattice distortion vary among alloy systems and processing routes.
A controlled comparison of composition-matched coarse- and fine-grained samples, with phase characterization and identical mechanical-test conditions, is proposed to test the hypothesis.
Failure of fine-grained samples to show a statistically significant increase in both hardness and yield strength is designated as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the hypothesis applies only when substantial precipitation is absent, whereas the falsification rule treats finding that improvements arose primarily from precipitation as falsification. Such a result instead places the experiment outside the hypothesis's stated applicability unless precipitation was independently shown to be negligible.
